title: POC weekly - latency tuning (rivermark)
summary: Weekly POC sync to review latency results and next tuning steps. Focus on improving TTFT via streaming config, evaluating new CUDA/ROCm kernels, and understanding sequence length distribution impact on batching; agreed next steps for benchmarks and a follow-up demo of streaming changes.
transcript:
Header:
Date: 2027-12-21
Start: 10:00 PST
Duration: ~45m
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Sara Patel (Rivermark Head of ML), Tom Nguyen (Rivermark Infra), Lena Brooks (Rivermark PM)

Auto-summary (auto-generated): quick sync on latency, some noisy transcription.

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for jumping on, um we got 45 minutes, main goals are quick review of the last run, TTFT numbers, and then action items. Diego will lead the perf bits.
[00:20] Diego: yep hi, thanks. quick note — we ran the new kernel set on the rig last night, and also flipped streaming on for a subset of routes. i'll share the raw results after.
[00:38] Sara: great, we've been seeing some outliers around 200–300ms tail on short queries, hoping to get that down.
[00:45] Diego: understood. first, TTFT—time to first token—improved with streaming on average by 60–80ms, but cold starts still spike because of model load. we also saw sequence length skew causing batching inefficiencies, like when a bunch of short prompts get mixed with long ones.
[01:12] Tom: on cold starts, are those from container spin-up or from kernel JIT?
[01:18] Diego: mainly model load and kernel warm-up, some JIT; on ROCm there was extra overhead on small seqs. NVIDIA kernels were faster for our seq profile, but we need to weigh vendor stack.
[01:33] Maya: quick question — are the tests using prefix/KV cache?
[01:36] Diego: yes, prefix cache enabled for the session tests, but not cross-request KV caching yet. that was deliberate to isolate streaming impacts.
[01:46] Lena: our typical user seq length is 24 tokens median, 128 95th, so most are short. we care about 95th p95 latency <= 150ms ideally.
[01:58] Diego: that distribution explains batching; short tokens means small compute, but batching waits for the batch window unless we use dynamic batching or imitate continuous batching.
[02:12] Maya: ok good — next, kernel choices. Diego, summarize the kernel matrix and the winners.
[02:19] Diego: sure. we profiled three kernel builds: baseline open-kernel v1 (generic), optimized-cu140 (nvidia-tuned), and our optimized-rocm patch. On the cluster we saw: nvidia-tuned best for short seqs (avg latency -18% vs baseline), open-kernel v1 was stable but slightly slower, rocm-perf was inconsistent — faster on long seqs but higher variance. also quantized int8 paths improved throughput but sometimes hurt TTFT a bit due to dequant overhead.
[02:52] Sara: so for our workload, nvidia-tuned wins?
[02:55] Diego: for latency yes, but cost and vendor lock-in considerations apply; we discussed fallback routing — if dedicated nodes are down, we can route to a more generic variant with slightly higher latency.
[03:07] Tom: about streaming — how did you configure chunk size and token flush? we saw some stuttering in the UI when chunks were too small.
[03:15] Diego: we used a 16-token chunk with immediate flush for the test. that reduced TTFT but increased total tokens sent, slight overhead. for your UI i'd recommend 32-token chunks with low-latency flush on first token, then coalesce next tokens for smoother UX.
[03:31] Lena: any impact on cost?
[03:33] Diego: streaming can increase token cost marginally; unit cost up <5% in our synthetic tests but UX improved. batching and KV cache lowered per-token compute which offsets some streaming cost.
[03:44] Maya: did we try prefix caching across sessions?
[03:47] Diego: not yet across sessions; we did intra-request KV reuse which helped tail latency on longer dialogues. cross-request caching requires sticky routing to keep KV locality.
[03:58] Sara: sticky routing is fine for pilot. security question — any change to data residency or logs when we enable streaming?
[04:04] Maya: no, streaming is just a delivery mechanism; logs and retention unchanged. we can also enable encryption-in-flight as usual.
[04:12] Tom: back to kernels — can you share the kernel perf spreadsheet?
[04:15] Diego: yes i'll upload. link will be in the notes. (brief pause) i also want to note that TTFT improvements were largest when we combined streaming + warm-backed model pool + nvidia-tuned kernel. that combo brought p50 TTFT from ~90ms to ~40ms on short prompts. p95 went from ~220ms to ~120ms.
[04:46] Sara: that's promising. for the canary we're planning 100 qps and mostly short prompts, any suggested config?
[04:53] Diego: recommended: dedicated nvidia-tuned pool, streaming enabled with 32-token initial flush, batch window 8–12ms, prefix cache enabled, 1 warm replica per 50 qps to reduce cold starts. autoscale policy with warm min will help.
[05:10] Lena: can you quantify the warm replica cost?
[05:13] Diego: roughly a 10–15% uplift vs purely burstable, depends on GPU type. we'll put numbers in the spreadsheet.
[05:19] Maya: action items we'll log. quick check — did we run the kernel tests with your real payloads (the ones with lots of markup)?
[05:28] Diego: yes we ran with two sets: synthetic short prompts and your sample corpus (doc snippets). the sample corpus had longer tail and negated some TTFT wins, so we need to tune chunking adaptively based on payload type.
[05:41] Sara: adaptive streaming, interesting. maybe route long-doc prompts to a non-stream path.
[05:46] Diego: exactly. that's a cheap policy to reduce extra token overhead on long docs.
[05:50] Tom: any infra blockers for trying the nvidia-tuned kernel on our staging?
[05:54] Diego: only access to a staging GPU cluster with compatible driver versions; need your infra to spin up 1 node for a few hours. we can do a rolling test.
[06:04] Tom: ok i'll try to provision. next — observability, did you capture token-level traces for the runs?
[06:10] Diego: yes we captured per-token latency and kernel call traces; i saw a couple of JIT events at ~3m into the longer runs.
[06:17] Maya: those JIT spikes correlate to model sharding events?
[06:19] Diego: more like kernel lazy compile on first use of certain ops. precompiling or using warmed images removes those.
[06:26] Lena: on next steps can we get a one-page recommended config for our SLA?
[06:30] Maya: yes we'll send a concise config doc.
[06:32] Sara: timeline — we want to start canary next week if possible.
[06:35] Maya: doable if infra provisioned. Diego, can you run one more end-to-end test with adaptive chunking and share the dashboard?
[06:41] Diego: yes i'll run tests tonight and share results tomorrow morning.
[06:44] Maya: perfect. any other questions?
[06:47] (brief crosstalk)
[07:00] Tom: small ask — can we get the sample payload workbook attached to the poc repo? makes it easier for infra to repro.
[07:06] Diego: will do.
[07:09] Maya: ok recap — share kernel perf spreadsheet, upload sample payloads, Diego to run adaptive chunk test and upload dashboard, Maya to produce one-page config for canary and cost estimate. schedule: let's meet same time next week.
[07:28] Lena: thanks all.
[07:30] End.

Notes: transcription contains some ASR errors around proper nouns, e.g., 'ROCm' sometimes transcribed as 'rock-em'. references: Kernel perf spreadsheet (link placeholder) https://redwood.internal/benchmarks/rivermark-kernels, canary config doc draft https://redwood.internal/docs/rivermark-canary
